title: cross-layer-failure-taxonomy-and-healing-playbook-2028
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary:
This document defines a cross-layer failure taxonomy for the Redwood serving runtime and prescribes a prioritized set of automated and manual healing patterns. It ties failure classes to observable signals, SLO impact estimates, kernel-scheduler interactions, and a validation protocol (simulation + benchmarks) to verify healing effectiveness. The goal is to reduce MTTI (mean time to impact resolution) and minimize customer-visible SLA violations while retaining explainability for operators and on-call engineers.

Scope:
- Systems covered: serving runtime (scheduler, kernel plugins, KV cache, model swapping path, request multiplexer), GPU nodes, and control-plane routing that affects inference.
- Not covered: provisioning infra (cloud provider account-level failures), storage backend outages unrelated to KV cache persistence.

Key definitions:
1) Failure mode: a discrete class of root cause (e.g., kernel starvation, KV cache thrash, model swap oscillation).
2) Signal: an observable metric or event correlated with a failure mode (e.g., per-gpu-run-queue-latency, kernel-backpressure-count).
3) Healing pattern: an automated or manual mitigation action (e.g., graceful model downgrade, preempt-and-slice, kernel rollback).

Cross-layer failure taxonomy (compact):
- Hardware Degradation:
  - Examples: NVLink flapping, thermal throttling, ECC corrections escalations leading to GPU driver resets.
  - Typical signals: thermal_temperature_gpu > 85C sustained, nvlink_error_rate > baseline, driver-restart events, unexpected GPU offline.
  - Immediate impact: abrupt token latency spikes, increased tail latency, node removal from pool.

- Kernel-level Regression / Latency Inflation:
  - Examples: new kernel release with suboptimal tiling for medium sequence length; per-kernel code-path takes 2x cycles for specific ops.
  - Signals: kernel_duration_p50/p95 increase for impacted kernel id, kernel-inflight-queued, kernel-error-ratio.
  - Interaction: scheduler may increase backpressure, leading to higher queueing latency across tenants.

- Scheduler Misconfiguration or Policy Conflict:
  - Examples: aggressive fairness policy resulting in starvation of high-priority SLOs; priority inversion with ephemeral plugins.
  - Signals: queue-depth-by-priority, delayed-scheduler-invocations, starvation-duration>threshold.

- KV cache evictions & cold-start storms:
  - Examples: bulk tenant requests after model swap cause cache churn and repeated warmups.
  - Signals: kvcache-hit-rate drop, warmup-requests-per-minute spike, per-request-additional-latency-with-warmup.

- Model-variant oscillation / continuous fallback churn:
  - Examples: routing policy repeatedly swaps between quantized and full-float model variants under marginal quality regressions.
  - Signals: model-switch-count, transient-quality-regression-alerts, per-session-inconsistency.

- Control-plane routing instability:
  - Examples: region-level routing flaps, misapplied rollout policy, bad canary rules.
  - Signals: route-change-events, sudden shift in capacity-utilization across regions, <route>-fallback-invoked.

Severity matrix and SLO correlation (short):
- Sev 1 (customer-impacting steady): sustained 50% increase in tail-99 latency, >5% error rate for >5 minutes.
- Sev 2 (degraded but partially functional): 20–50% tail-99 increase, transient errors affecting <5% of requests.
- Sev 3 (anomalous but within SLO): localized kernel latency bump, single-node thermal throttling with graceful failover.

Observable signals catalog (recommended):
- infra.*: gpu_temp_celsius, nvlink_errors, driver_restarts, node_oom_kills
- kernel.*: kernel_exec_time_ms{kernel_id}, kernel_error_count, kernel-inflight
- scheduler.*: queue_depth{priority}, time_to_schedule_ms, preemptions_per_minute
- kvcache.*: hit_rate, warmup_ops_per_minute, eviction_rate
- model.*: model_swap_count, variant_latency_ms, quality_regression_delta
- request.*: per_request_tail_latency_ms{p50,p95,p99}, request_error_rate

Automated healing patterns (ordered by safety):
1) Protective throttling and admission control (safe):
   - When queue_depth{all} > Q_HI and p99_latency > L_HI, trigger per-tenant admission-shed at 5–20% increments with exponential backoff.
   - Purpose: immediately reduce queuing amplification and allow kernels to drain.

2) Kernel safety-net rollback (safe with guardrails):
   - Trigger conditions: kernel_exec_time_p95 exceeds baseline * 1.6 AND kernel_error_increase > X.
   - Action: flip the kernel feature-flag to the previous stable kernel variant on affected shard group; increment kernel-rollback-counter; notify runtime-ops.
   - Validation: quick microbenchmark run (10s, sample requests) against canary path to confirm p95 return.

3) Model variant staged fallback (safe for quality):
   - Trigger: model_latency_multiplier > 1.5 OR kvcache-hit-rate < 0.2 for > 30s.
   - Action: route new requests to a fallback variant (quantized or smaller context) using session-preserving redirect; enable quality-guardrail sampling for first 100 requests.

4) KV cache conservative mode & priming (safe):
   - Action steps: reduce cache target size for new sessions, enable proactive priming background job for top-N prefixes, temporarily exempt high-SLA tenants from eviction until priming completes.

5) Node isolation & graceful eviction (higher disruption):
   - If node-level GPU errors or thermal thresholds persist, mark node in draining state; initiate graceful eviction of live sessions with session-transfer when supported; prevent new allocations for 5 minutes; coordinate with fleet-autorepair.

6) Scheduler quick-slice preemption (experimental):
   - Use when kernel-backed stalls cause broad queueing but kernels still launch. Create short preemption slices (50–100ms) to interleave low-latency tenants. Only enabled under controlled flags and rollouts.

Decision heuristics and guardrails:
- Do not perform model-variant fallback if quality-monitoring signals show >2% quality degradation in last 30s.
- Kernel rollback requires at least one successful microbenchmark verification and should record an audit event with a trace id.
- Admission-shed must be tenant-scoped and rate-limited; global sheds are an emergency-only action.

Manual triage and runbook (for on-call):
1) Initial detection (0–5 minutes):
   - Pull SLO dashboard for affected route/model.
   - Check node health (gpu_temp_celsius, driver_restarts), kernel errors, and scheduler queue depths.
2) Quick containment (5–15 minutes):
   - If spike is noise, observe for additional 5 minutes.
   - If persistent, enable tenant-scoped admission-shed at 10% and monitor p99.
3) If kernel regression suspected (15–30 minutes):
   - Trigger kernel-rollback play (via runtime admin cli): runtime-admin rollback-kernel --shard-group <id> --cause "p95-regression-<id>"
   - Run microbenchmark: bench-tool --target sh://<shard> --template warmup_short --duration 10s
4) If KV cache storm (15–45 minutes):
   - Apply kvcache-conservative-mode for affected shards: runtime-admin set-kvcache-mode --shards <list> --mode conservative
   - Kick off priming job: priming-svc start --strategy top-prefixes --window 10m
5) Escalate to runtime-core if cross-shard rollback needed or if node isolation fails.

Kernel scheduling interactions (guidance):
- Preemption semantics: preemption should avoid inflight KV mutations; prefer slice boundaries at request or token boundaries where possible.
- Batching trade-offs: increased batching increases throughput but amplifies kernel regressions across tenants; include batch-size hysteresis in scheduler policy to quickly reduce batch size on p95 inflation.
- Priority inversion detection: monitor latency deltas by priority band; automated alert if p95_low_priority improves while p95_high_priority worsens beyond threshold.

Simulation & validation recipe (must-run for any new healing policy):
1) Test harness: use the operational workload simulator with a blended-client-corpus (from request-surface-replay) and inject fault primitives (thermal_increase, kernel_slowdown_x2, kvcache-eviction-spike).
2) Benchmarks to run:
   - pre/post p95/p99 delta test (steady state 5m window)
   - tail amplification ratio under 5% error injection
   - model-quality-sampling to validate fallback fidelity (1000 sampled completions compared via eval-set).
3) Success criteria: automated healing must reduce p99 to <=1.2x baseline within 120s for Sev2 and within 300s for Sev1 while quality regression remains within policy bounds.
4) Regression checks: ensure no >0.5% increased error surface for unrelated tenants during tests.

Operational playbook for release validation (Autonomous Recovery v1):
- Feature description: Autonomous Recovery v1 implements kernel-rollback, kvcache-conservative-mode, and tenant-scoped admission-shed as coordinated automated responses.
- Staged rollout: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 3 days with automated rollback on predefined SLO regressions.
- Acceptance tests for each stage: run the simulation recipe for 15m and confirm success criteria.
- Rollback criteria: p99 latency regression > 1.5x baseline OR quality-sampling failure > 2% in two consecutive windows.

Telemetry and observability additions required:
- Add a healing-events stream: healing_event{type, target, trigger, actor, trace_id}.
- Annotate request traces with healing_hint when fallback/rollback applied.
- Add a dashboard: "Healing Effectiveness" showing time-to-heal histograms, success-rate by type, and per-tenant impact.

Troubleshooting checklist (fast):
- If rollback didn't reduce p95: verify microbenchmark runner executed against same shard; confirm kernel-side metrics were ingested.
- If admission-shed did not apply: confirm policy sync to edge routing; check policy-eval-latency.
- If kvcache priming thrashed memory: inspect priming job concurrency and rate-limit to avoid OOM.

Ownership & escalation:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: runtime-oncall@redwood.com).
- Secondary: eng-sre (pager: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com).
- Escalation path: on-call -> runtime-core -> infra-platform lead -> engineering director.

Appendix A — Example CLI snippets:
- Rollback kernel:
  runtime-admin rollback-kernel --shard-group sg-17 --kernel-id k-2027-11 --reason "p95_regression_20270302"
- Set kvcache conservative mode:
  runtime-admin set-kvcache-mode --shards sg-17,sg-18 --mode conservative --ttl 10m
- Start priming job:
  priming-svc start --strategy top-prefixes --sample-size 500 --shard sg-17

Appendix B — Minimal YAML policy sample (human-readable):
  healingPolicies:
    - name: kernel-safety-net-v1
      conditions:
        - metric: kernel_exec_time_p95
          comparator: ">"
        - threshold: 1.6
      actions:
        - type: rollback-kernel
          cooldown: 120s
